found: Measured: after the reboot the agent replayed the afternoon's jobs from the oldest (102 started, 40 ok, 62 failed - mostly guards refusing), fifty at a time after a reconnect, on shared clones; it had inferred 'pending' from a missing result. Before that it stalled at 22:29 CET with nothing logged until the reboot. No alert could reach the author - every channel went through the agent. Harm: none - four replayed pull requests, all the legitimate tad 0.4.0 pin bump; no direct pushes, tags, releases or phone actions; tools and clones restored. The root: a job is a script with no record of its life. Proven answers: durable execution's event history and heartbeats (Temporal), leases with fencing tokens (Kleppmann; Patterns of Distributed Systems), a dead man's switch watched from elsewhere (Healthchecks), crash-only recovery (Candea and Fox), run-once jobs with deadlines (Kubernetes), idempotency keys (Stripe), a working tree per job (git worktree). Replayed 2026-11-12: the old agent's real log of 2026-11-11, read line by line through oco-agent's rules (oco-agent/replay): of the 357 jobs the old agent started over six runs, oco-agent would have started 255 and refused exactly 102, each because it had already finished - the first at 23:16:24, the moment the replay began. The journal it kept (764 rows of tad data) checks out and answers SQL. 2026-11-12, from the whole system's log: the machine did not sleep and its network stayed up through the stall; a USB device was disconnected at 22:25:28 with nothing after it going wrong, so the phone looks innocent. The stall was inside lab-agent's daemon. Its GitHub client is built with no limit on how long a request may take (src/github.rs: ureq::AgentBuilder::new().build()), so one connection that hangs holds the polling loop for ever - which fits every fact, though nobody watched it hang. oco-agent's client limits every request to 20 s. The desktop is set to suspend after an hour without input, and lab-agent keeps it awake only while a job runs. 2026-11-12, proven: the replays come from lab-agent's reading of what is done. already_handled lists its results folder through GitHub's contents API, which returns at most 1,000 entries and says nothing of the rest: the folder held 1,135; the first replayed job of the second replay (1794436981-after-reconnect) had its result, but was not among the 1,000 listed. Every job past the thousandth looked unfinished. Both replays - 102 jobs on 2026-11-11 and 25 after the boot on 2026-11-12 - share this one cause. The 2026-11-12 replay changed no repository (no commits since the boot) but put tad 0.4.0 back on the lab (restored to 0.5.0). 2026-11-12, later - the stall is proven too, and it has the same cause as the replays. lab-agent sees new jobs through the same contents listing of its jobs folder, cut silently at 1,000 entries. The folder holds a placeholder, .keep, which sorts before every job; when lab-agent started its last job before the stall (22:29:23), the folder held 999 jobs - with .keep, exactly 1,000. Every job submitted after that lay past the end of the listing: the agent was alive, polling, and blind. The earlier note here that a request with no time limit was the probable cause was wrong as the main cause; time limits are added anyway, since a hang should never be silent either. One cause - a listing that stops without a word - made the stall, the replay of 102 jobs, and the replay of 25 after the boot.
question: What let the 2026-11-11 incident happen, and how do proven systems prevent each part of it?

found: PURPOSE - best: say why a thing exists and what it must reach in terms that can be checked, and few of them. Keeps: the idea, milestones with criteria and readiness. Lacks: nothing essential. KNOWLEDGE - best: every claim with its source, and a question before an answer. Keeps: research, sources, concepts, vocabulary. Lacks: how a finding is known - measured, read, or reasoned; on 2026-11-12 a reasoned guess (a request with no time limit) stood beside measured facts and was wrong. REASONING - best: a decision on one page with its context, what was rejected, its consequences and its status (Toyota's A3, Nygard's decision records). Keeps: decisions with why, rejected, research, sources. Lacks: the relation between decisions - one refining or replacing another is written as text today, three times on 2026-11-12. WORK - best: visible flow, pull, limits, ageing (Kanban, Reinertsen). Keeps: the backlog's flow, driver, next, since, waits_on; oco-agent's journal says what actually ran. Lacks: why this work - its link to the milestone or decision it serves. RESULTS - best: evidence that can be checked, not a claim. Keeps: glimpses, workings with evidence, gathered releases, activity and test runs. Lacks: evidence as a link to the thing that proves it. LOOKING BACK - best: the After Action Review, hansei. Keeps: reflections. Lacks: nothing essential. PROBLEMS - best: the andon - a problem visible the moment it happens, to everyone, until it is dealt with. Keeps: nothing of its own; attention is computed for the flow only. Lacks: the lens itself - 21 release runs failed unseen and a watcher was silent for a night on 2026-11-12. The largest gap. INVITATION - best: a need marked where it is, small and well-defined, fillable by whoever passes (Wikipedia's citation needed, good-first-issue labels, citizen science, device owners filling a support table). Keeps: nothing. Lacks: the entity - what is needed, of what kind (information, a test on a device, feedback), where, and how to give it. What open commons add to Toyota's room. THE SKY ITSELF - what makes lenses one dome: relations seen as connections, the story, and time. Keeps: about 860 links that resolve, the essence a star tells, and history in git. Lacks: the relations declared - the dome's continuity rests on them. So, in order: declare the relations (among them one decision refining another, and work serving a milestone); the problems lens; the invitation; how a finding is known and evidence that links; then lenses as data.
question: Lens by lens, what does the best of the world's experience say - stripped of ceremony - and what does ocoeco keep or lack for it?

found: The best of it is Toyota's obeya, the big room: begun on the Prius project because no single person held the knowledge the work needed, its walls showed purpose, plan, progress, problems and countermeasures together, so that anyone entering saw the whole and problems became visible. Around it: make things visible (mieruka), signal a problem at once (andon), go and see the real thing, pull work rather than push it, a decision on one page with its reasoning (A3), and look back (hansei). What was added later - command centres, score boards, points, ceremonies - is the part to leave out. A board, then, is not a list of tasks: it is the room, and a flow of work is one of its walls. ocoeco's entities already are those walls: the idea and milestones (purpose); research, sources, concepts and words (knowledge); decisions with what was rejected (reasoning); the backlog's flow (work); glimpses, workings and their evidence (results); reflections (looking back); what needs attention (problems). Open commons need one wall Toyota's room never did: there nobody is assigned, so the room must also invite - show what is needed from whoever comes: a piece of information, a test on a device, feedback. Ostrom found commons last where those who use a thing can see its state and take part in its rules.
question: What is a board, taking the best of the world's experience and leaving its ceremony out - and what is it for open commons?
